elements.text: our own data · our own rules

beats.title: A new “best” every week
beats.notes: Every week a new AI model claims to be the best.

beats.title: Best for what?
beats.notes: But best on whose data? Best for which job? And best at what price?

beats.title: Why we built LLM Lab
beats.notes: We built LLM Lab so we can answer those questions ourselves, with our own data and by our own rules.

beats.title: Three ways to choose
beats.notes: Most companies choose models in one of three ways: a public leaderboard, a vendor’s sales deck, or whatever the first team happened to use.

beats.title: One shared weakness
beats.notes: All three share one weakness: the test wasn’t ours.

elements.text: their documents · their languages · their idea of “good”

beats.title: Someone else's data
beats.notes: A public benchmark measures someone else’s documents, someone else’s languages and someone else’s idea of “good”.

beats.title: English vs Polish
beats.notes: A model that tops the charts in English may struggle with Polish support tickets.

beats.title: Two points, thirty times the price
beats.notes: A model that’s two points better might cost thirty times more.

beats.title: Nobody re-checks
beats.notes: And once a model is in production, nobody checks whether it’s still the right choice.

beats.title: Our data. Our criteria. Our decision.
beats.notes: That’s what sovereignty means here. We’re not building our own models. We’re owning the decision.

beats.title: Our data
beats.notes: Our data. The test cases come from our own work: real support questions, real contracts, real tickets. They live in our own repository and get reviewed like code.

beats.title: Our criteria
beats.notes: Our criteria. We decide what “good enough” means. For detecting personal data the bar is high, because a miss is a compliance incident. For product search it can be lower.

beats.title: Our decision
beats.notes: Our decision. A model we call through an API and a model we host ourselves face exactly the same tests. If a provider raises prices or changes its terms, we already know our next-best option and what it costs.

beats.title: Four types of models
beats.notes: We’re starting with four types of models, the building blocks behind search, assistants and automation:

beats.title: Embedding
beats.notes: Embedding models turn text into numbers, so we can find the documents that match a question.

beats.title: Chunking
beats.notes: Chunking splits long documents into pieces that make sense on their own.

beats.title: Reranking
beats.notes: Reranking takes the top search results and puts the best answer first.

beats.title: Classification
beats.notes: Classification sorts incoming items: what the customer wants, how urgent it is, whether the message contains personal data.

beats.title: Built to grow
beats.notes: More categories will follow. The lab is built to grow.

beats.title: RAG in one picture
beats.notes: This is a RAG system: retrieval-augmented generation. It has two lanes. At the back, indexing happens offline, before anyone asks anything. At the front, a question comes in and gets answered live. Our three model types sit in exactly these two lanes.

beats.title: Chunking: cut the documents
beats.notes: First, chunking. In the indexing lane, our documents are cut into small pieces that make sense on their own. Without good chunks, the system can only retrieve half a thought.

beats.title: Embedding: chunks become vectors
beats.notes: Next, embedding. Each chunk is turned into a vector, a list of numbers that captures its meaning, and stored in the vector database. This is still offline work, done once and updated when documents change.

beats.title: Embedding again, at query time
beats.notes: Now a user asks a question. The same embedding model turns the question into a vector, and the vector database returns the chunks closest to it. That is why the embedding model must be the same at both ends.

beats.title: Reranking: best chunk first
beats.notes: Search returns many candidates, and the best one is not always on top. Reranking looks at them again and sorts them by relevance, so the model sees the strongest evidence first.

beats.title: The LLM writes the answer
beats.notes: Finally the top chunks go to the large language model, which writes the answer. Chunking, embedding and reranking decide what the model gets to read, so each of them is worth testing on our own data.

beats.title: Three numbers
beats.notes: Every model gets just three numbers: quality on our tests, cost per thousand tasks, and speed.

beats.title: Everything else left out
beats.notes: We left out everything else, because those three are what we actually choose on.

beats.title: Four answers
beats.notes: From them, the lab gives four answers for every category: best quality, best value, cheapest and fastest.

beats.title: Quality against cost
beats.notes: Here’s classification. The chart shows quality against cost, and up and to the left is better.

beats.title: The quality bar
beats.notes: The dashed line is our quality bar. Anything below it isn’t recommended, however cheap it is.

beats.title: ModernBERT looks great
beats.notes: This fine-tuned model is a good example. On average it looks great, and it costs a tiny fraction of the alternatives.

beats.title: But not on personal data
beats.notes: But on personal-data detection it falls below the minimum we set, so the lab won’t recommend it as our one classifier for everything.

beats.title: Support intents only
beats.notes: Now look at intent detection alone. Here it becomes the cheapest and fastest choice.

beats.title: Use it where it's strong
beats.notes: It’s the same data with a more precise question: use the model where it’s strong.

beats.title: Scores with ranges
beats.notes: The lab is also honest about uncertainty. Every score comes with a range.

beats.title: Within range = tie
beats.notes: When two models are within that range of each other, the lab calls it a tie

beats.title: Decide on cost or speed
beats.notes: and tells us to decide on cost or speed, instead of paying for a difference that isn’t real.

elements.text: no model scores higher because it has seen the answers

beats.title: Test sets: scoring only
beats.notes: Finally, the data itself. Test sets are used only for scoring.

beats.title: Training sets: fine-tuning only
beats.notes: Training sets are used only for fine-tuning,

beats.title: Checked for overlap
beats.notes: and they’re checked for overlap with the test sets, so no model scores higher just because it has already seen the answers.

beats.title: Decisions we can explain
beats.notes: This gives us decisions we can explain.

beats.title: Not “top of a leaderboard”
beats.notes: When someone asks “why this model?”, the answer isn’t “it was top of a leaderboard”.

beats.title: Our tests, our data, this price
beats.notes: It’s: it passed our tests, on our data, at this price, and here’s the evidence.

beats.title: New model? Run it.
beats.notes: And when a new model comes out, we add it, run it, and the lab shows us whether it’s worth switching.
